column3: Making a word remain among descendants gives a limited contrast to making idols into fragments so people may return to the remaining one.
Joseph's prayer to the Creator and guardian does not clarify the staged breaking of the idols.
The uncut gift forms a lexical and conceptual contrast to the deliberately cut idols.
Signs and punishment intended to prompt return offer only a broad counterpart to the focus's engineered return to the largest idol.
The gift of criterion to Moses and Aaron does not add to Ibrahim's immediate evidence scene.
Divine power to return a person is a different sense of return from redirecting an inquiry to an idol.
Making attackers like eaten straw supplies an independent image of a collective reduced to remnants.
Ibrahim's testimony that the Creator is their Lord supplies the theological claim behind his challenge to the idols.
The sky's recurring return does not clarify the narrative return built into the focus scene.
Joseph's deliberate placement of goods to induce recognition and return usefully parallels a placed object designed to elicit a response.
The opening question about the images establishes the idol practice that the fragmentation exposes.
The great seizure and vengeance do not develop the broken-idol inquiry.
Lesser punishment intended to prompt return offers only a general corrective-return pattern.
The demand for a made god beside a people devoted to idols gives a relevant wider instance of fabricated worship.
A great plot has no focused connection to the arrangement of broken idols.
The great divine favor promised to believers does not clarify the focus.
Fear of the unseen Lord and the Hour does not add to the idol-breaking scene.
Return to the Lord is not the local return of a question to the surviving idol.
Continued delivery of the word for remembrance gives only distant background for a scene meant to provoke recognition.
The community's immediate question, "Who did this to our gods?", begins the investigation that the remaining idol directs.
The comparison of worldly and final punishment does not clarify the focus's material arrangement.
The greatness of divine favor is unrelated to the one large idol left standing.
Ibrahim's announced plan against the idols is the immediate intention fulfilled by the focus ayah.
Awaiting what envoys bring back is a different return, with only a faint response-pattern parallel.
Divine transcendence above their sayings does not add to the staged evidence.
Remembering and seeing after temptation offers a remote analogue of recognition, without the idol scene.
Arrogant nighttime talk does not clarify the fragmentation or its intended inquiry.
Coming submissively when right is on one's side does not illuminate the focus.
The blessed reminder and its rejection provide immediate surah context for the contrast between revelation and idol devotion.
A deliberately delivered letter followed by withdrawal to observe the response parallels the focus's controlled provocation of an answer.
The Quran's guidance and great reward do not add to this idol-breaking episode.
The report identifying Ibrahim as the youth who mentioned the gods advances the public inquiry caused by the damage.
Worldly disgrace and greater final punishment do not clarify the focus's evidence scene.
A made vision as a trial offers only a broad parallel to a deliberately arranged test.
Resurrection-day correction and patterned examples do not explain the broken idols.
Great dominion in paradise has no focused link to the remaining large idol.
Return to God and accounting do not clarify the local narrative maneuver.
Ibrahim's prior sound judgment identifies the discernment governing his planned act.
The distinction between those who respond and the unresponsive dead offers only a distant contrast to the people failing the idol test.
The exclusive call to worship God supplies the doctrinal standard against which the idols are shown powerless.
Bringing Ibrahim before public witnesses turns the broken-idol scene into the public examination it was designed to produce.
Return to God for accounting is not a useful reading of the focus's local return.
The claim that guidance risks expulsion and the provision of fruit do not add to the focus.
Persistent rejection of examples gives distant background for the community's inability to read the evidence before them.
Mutual blame at judgment does not clarify the immediate inquiry about the idols.
Moses's return to a people engaged in calf worship is a distant idol-related episode, but does not advance this staged breakage.
The people's appeal to inherited idol worship supplies the commitment that Ibrahim's act puts under examination.
Pharaoh's elite arrogance does not clarify the focus scene.
Ibrahim explicitly assigns the act to the largest idol and commands inquiry of the idols, completing the focus ayah's intended setup.
The direct accusation of Ibrahim is the next necessary step in the inquiry prepared by the focus.
The return of all affairs to God does not explain the return of this question to an idol.
Detailed signs so people may return provide a broad corrective purpose, without the focus's specific device.
Making an angel appear as a man does not clarify making idols into pieces.
Fearful believers expecting return to their Lord do not add to the focus.
The cutting apart of a matter among people gives a limited formal contrast to the cutting apart of the idols.
Ibrahim's verdict that the people and their ancestors are plainly astray states the judgment his action makes visible.
The greatest overwhelming event does not clarify the surviving large idol.
Destroyed surrounding towns and varied signs offer a broad warning-and-return pattern only.
The charge that these objects can neither benefit nor harm articulates the incapacity exposed by their being broken and questioned.
The greatest sign shown to Pharaoh does not clarify the focus's large idol.
Scattering communities and testing them for return gives only a remote fragmentation-and-return resonance.
The question whether any creator besides God provides sustenance reinforces the Creator claim against fabricated gods.
The instruction to return from a house is unrelated to returning a question to an idol.
Destroying ships for what people earned does not clarify the focus.
The people's question whether Ibrahim brings truth or play names the ambiguity his disruptive act is meant to force them to confront.
Seeing great signs does not develop the idol-breaking inquiry.
A people left motionless after an earthquake is a distant destruction image, not a reading of the focus.
The command to burn Ibrahim in support of the gods reveals the supporters' response after their gods' impotence is exposed.
The soul's return to its Lord is unrelated to the local evidentiary return.
The destruction of plotters and their people offers a compact consequence for an attempted plot, though it is not the focus's setup.
Seeing an evil deed as good offers a limited analogue to the community's distorted attachment to idols.
Return to God for disclosure does not clarify the focus scene.
This repeats the distant earthquake-destruction image already supplied by 7:78.
The fire's reversal preserves Ibrahim against the retaliation provoked by his act, completing the episode's reversal of power.
Human-caused corruption and partial tasting of consequences for return offer only a general corrective frame.
Creation of people and pairs does not clarify the intentional cutting of the idols.
Fighting oath-breaking leaders to make them desist does not add to the focus.
Their return to themselves and admission of wrongdoing is the self-testimony the staged question draws out.
Expectation of returning to the Lord does not clarify the inquiry's redirected return.
The attempted plot against Ibrahim is reversed into loss for its authors, extending the episode's reversal of apparent power.
Refusal to return in blindness and deafness does not add to the focus.
At death, false objects of invocation vanish and people testify against themselves, a distant counterpart to exposed powerless gods.
Pharaoh's arrogant denial of return to God gives only a broad arrogance-and-accountability parallel.
After recognizing that the idols cannot speak, they reverse again into evasive speech; this marks the failure of the inquiry to reform them.
A strategy to induce others to turn back is a remote procedural parallel to provoking a response.
Ibrahim's rebuke of the worshippers and their powerless objects states the conclusion of the evidence scene.
Varied warnings meant to produce reverence or remembrance give only general admonitory context.
Written exhortation and the fate of the defiantly sinful do not clarify the focus.
The faithful response to calamity and return to God is not a reading of the broken-idol scene.
Ibrahim's later deliverance with Lot situates the aftermath of the episode, but adds little to the central evidence device.
The accusation that a messenger is mad does not clarify the focus.
Covenant-breaking and hardened hearts do not add to this idol-breaking inquiry.
Scattered dust gives a concise image of disintegration, but without the focus's intentional arrangement and surviving exception.
Divine knowledge of private counsel and later disclosure does not clarify the focus.
The known appointed time does not add to the focus.
The account of magic and its harms does not clarify the broken-idol evidence scene.
Pharaoh's accusation about Moses's past act does not add to the focus.
Rules of modesty and repentance do not clarify the focus.
Household etiquette does not add to the focus.
The isolated opening letters do not provide a usable link to the focus.
Ibrahim's rejection of his father's idols is an essential earlier formulation of the anti-idol reasoning enacted in 21:58.
The question whether associates can create anything while being created directly exposes the false agency that the surviving idol is made to display.
The idols' inability to help either worshippers or themselves gives the central incapacity demonstrated by their fragmentation.
Calling idols that cannot follow or answer closely anticipates the challenge to ask the largest idol if it can speak.
The command to call alleged partners and await their response gives a direct wider parallel to redirecting the question to the remaining idol.
The inventory of powerless limbs and senses directly clarifies why neither the broken idols nor their largest companion can answer.
Objects that neither hear a call nor see their worshippers provide a close formulation of the speech test in the episode.
The calf, treated as a body that cannot speak or guide, offers a close alternative instance of manufactured worship exposed by its incapacity.
Recognition that the calf neither speaks nor directs closely parallels the realization Ibrahim forces concerning the idols.
The failure of invoked gods to avail their people at destruction extends the focus's exposure of powerless objects into its consequence.
Joseph's refusal to follow what his forefathers worship besides God provides a parallel rejection of inherited devotion.
Ibrahim's prayer that he and his descendants be kept from worshipping idols names the enduring stakes of his confrontation.
Those called besides God create nothing and are themselves created, reinforcing the Creator-versus-made-object contrast.
Dead, unaware objects cannot meet a demand for speech or agency, making this a useful counterpart to the focus scene.
Objects invoked besides God cannot remove or alter harm, clarifying the claimed gods' practical impotence.
The demand for authority for gods besides God frames the evidentiary deficiency behind the community's inherited worship.
Ibrahim asks why his father worships what neither hears nor sees nor benefits, directly anticipating the focus's speech test.
The warning not to worship Satan contrasts obedient worship with the false allegiance embodied in the idols.
The fashioned calf presented as a god gives a close example of a made body falsely assigned divine status.
The calf's inability to answer speech or control harm and benefit directly parallels the incapacity exposed by the remaining idol.
The demand for proof for gods besides God supplies the argumentative standard enacted by Ibrahim's arranged evidence.
Those invoked besides God cannot create even a fly or recover what it takes, a compact and direct statement of idol incapacity.
False gods that create nothing, cannot control harm or benefit, and lack power over death or life closely illuminate the focus's test.
Ibrahim's question, "What do you worship?", opens the same interrogation of idol devotion developed in 21:52-67.
The answer that they worship idols and remain devoted to them supplies the attachment that the focus disrupts.
The question whether idols hear when called is a direct parallel to asking the surviving idol to speak.
The question whether idols benefit or harm names the practical incapacity exposed through their breakage.
The appeal to ancestral practice parallels the defenders' inherited rationale in 21:53.
Ibrahim's invitation to examine the objects worshipped by them and their forefathers advances the same evidentiary challenge.
Ibrahim's command to worship God and be mindful of Him provides the positive alternative to idol devotion.
The statement that idols neither provide provision nor merit worship directly reinforces their exposed powerlessness.
Those called besides God cannot hear, cannot answer even if they heard, and deny the association later; it is a close general parallel to 21:63.
People take gods besides God seeking help, a motive overturned when the gods cannot preserve even themselves.
Ibrahim's question about what the people worship is a direct parallel interrogation of idolatry.
The rejection of false gods beside God supplies the doctrinal judgment behind the physical challenge to the idols.
Ibrahim's turning toward the gods immediately precedes another closely related act against idol bodies.
His question, "Why do you not speak?", is the exact incapacity that 21:58 is arranged to expose.
Striking the idols supplies the nearest narrative counterpart to reducing them to pieces.
The question whether they worship what they carve explicitly contrasts human manufacture with divine worthiness.
God's creation of people and what they make completes the Creator-versus-fabricated-object contrast.
The opponents' move to build and burn Ibrahim parallels the retaliatory escalation in 21:68.
Their plot against Ibrahim and its reversal extends the same episode-level conflict and reversal of power.
The confession that God created the heavens and earth sharpens the inconsistency of turning from the Creator to powerless objects.
Ibrahim's declaration of dissociation from what his people worship provides a compact precursor to his action in 21:58.
His exception for the One who created him states the Creator-centered alternative to fabricated worship.
None is more astray than one who calls on beings that will not answer until the Day and are unaware of the call, closely matching the focus's speech test.
Ibrahim's disavowal of his people's worship and declaration of enmity until belief in God gives the communal boundary underlying the confrontation.
